Solomon, Rabb applaud House passage of semi primaries legislation
Rep. Christopher M. Rabb
September 30, 2026 | 3:10 PM
HARRISBURG, Sept. 30 –
This week, state Reps. Jared Solomon and Chris Rabb applaud the House of Representatives for advancing House Bill 280, which would allow for an open primary election system in Pennsylvania, by a 115-88 vote.
The bill would allow unaffiliated voters to participate in the primary. At least 40 states have some form of semi-open primaries. According to the Pennsylvania Department of State, there are more than 1.5 million Pennsylvanians not affiliated with either of the two major political parties.
“1.5 million voters have no voice or vote in the primary system in PA,” Solomon said. “For the first time ever we had the full House vote to bring independents into civic life in Pennsylvania.”
Rabb said that no Pennsylvanian should be treated as a second-class citizen or have their constitutional right to vote undermined by state law.
“Ensuring a full and equal electorate is a just way to strengthen our democracy,” Rabb said. “With this bill, independent voters can express their preference in local, state, and federal elections and make a real impact on how their communities function. I encourage the Senate to give this sizable portion of our electorate a real voice in primary elections.”
H.B. 280 will now head to the Senate for consideration.
More information on the bill is available at:
https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb280
.

Rabb introduces legislation to reduce stolen, lost firearms from federally licensed dealers
Rep. Christopher M. Rabb
September 29, 2026 | 10:27 AM
HARRISBURG, Sept. 29
– This week, state Rep. Chris Rabb introduced House Bill 2808, seeking to reduce the number of firearms stolen or lost from federally licensed dealers.
The bill, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, would require the Pennsylvania State Police or their designees to conduct annual inspections of federally licensed firearms dealers and would codify a duty to report lost or stolen firearms or ammunition.
Two programs would also be established via H.B. 2808: one to provide grants to dealers to modernize their operations and another to fund PSP-led recruitment, training and oversight of designees who verify that dealers properly store and secure firearms sales records.
“With over 3,000 federally licensed firearms dealers across the state, we need to identify which are complicit in the flow of illegal firearms, while providing ample support for the good-faith dealers seeking modernization,” Rabb said. “By empowering law enforcement and their designees to inspect gun dealers, without infringing on Pennsylvanians’ Second Amendment rights, we’re making our streets safer for everyone.”
State Reps. Jen Mazzocco (D-Allegheny) and Lindsay Powell (D-Allegheny), two co-sponsors of the bill, echoed the need for sensible illegal firearm legislation.
“With H.B. 2808, Pennsylvania can keep licensed firearms dealers running efficiently while finding real solutions to the scourge of gun violence in our communities,” Mazzocco said. “This is a way to take more illegal firearms off the streets just by reaffirming laws that are already on the books, and I hope my colleagues join in this reform.”
“Illegal firearms have been an epidemic across our state, and it is time we enact reforms to address this and find where the most common root of this problem lies,” Powell said. “House Bill 2808 will ensure that we do not have to choose between the safety of our communities and protecting Second Amendment rights, and I look forward to seeing this commonsense legislation move forward.”
More information on the bill is available at:
https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb2808
.

Rabb introduces legislation to uphold religious neutrality in schools
Rep. Christopher M. Rabb
September 16, 2026 | 2:47 PM
HARRISBURG, Sept. 16
– Today, state Rep. Chris Rabb introduced H.B. 2776,
also known as the Promoting Liberty & Upholding Rights of All Learners (PLURAL) Act.
The bill would establish clear standards to uphold religious neutrality in public schools and define appropriate boundaries for religious activity in educational settings, making clear that instruction remains academically free from endorsement or denigration of any belief system.
The legislation would also reinforce that violations of protections constitute unlawful discrimination under the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act and would provide a pathway for enforcement and accountability.
“With students across Pennsylvania navigating increasingly complex social and cultural environments, we need to do our part to keep public schools as spaces of inclusivity and respect,” said Rabb, D-Phila. “Moreover, learning environments should be grounded in constitutional protections, protecting the rights of students regardless of their faith, beliefs, or nonbelief. This bill will establish clear guidance for the commonwealth’s education system reflecting our shared commitment to equity.”
Co-sponsor Rep. Tarah Probst, D-Monroe/Pike, said that she strongly supports the PLURAL Act “because our public schools should be welcoming and inclusive spaces for every student and family.”
“When taxpayer dollars fund our schools, those dollars come from Pennsylvanians of many faiths, cultures, traditions and beliefs – as well as those who practice no religion,” Probst said. “Our public institutions should remain religiously neutral, ensuring that no student’s tax dollars are used to promote or impose a particular religious belief. This principle is rooted in Pennsylvania’s constitution, which, through Article I, Section 3, protects freedom of conscience and prohibits government from compelling religious support or giving preference to any religious establishment.”
For more information on H.B. 2776, those interested can visit
https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb2776

Rabb secures $750,000 for Sedgwick Theatre renovations
Rep. Christopher M. Rabb
September 15, 2026 | 11:47 AM
PHILADELPHIA, Sept. 15
– Today, state Rep. Chris Rabb announced that $750,000 in funding from the state Department of Community & Economic Development’s Local Share Account will go toward an elevator renovation project at the Sedgwick Theater.
The LSA funding will cover a majority of the project, which would install two new elevators at the historic theater originally opened in 1928 at 7137 Germantown Ave. Funding for this and other LSA projects in Pennsylvania is provided by the distribution of gaming revenues by the Commonwealth Financing Authority.
The project will support a front passenger elevator that will connect the basement, first and second floors of the theater for patrons, artists and attendees, as well as community groups and residents that rent the space for gatherings. Renovations will also include a rear service elevator to facilitate the movement of chairs, risers, props and other items across all three floors.
“It’s been exciting to see the plans made at the Sedgwick to better facilitate live performances and increase accessibility for patrons,” Rabb said. “This theater has been in the lives of Philadelphians for generations, and I’m proud to secure funding that will keep this treasure of the district thriving as a creative environment.”
More information about LSA programs is available here:
https://dced.pa.gov/programs/local-share-account-lsa-statewide/

Rabb introduces legislation to establish Equal Opportunity Audit program
Rep. Christopher M. Rabb
September 14, 2026 | 11:22 AM
PHILADELPHIA, Sept. 14
– This past week, state Rep. Chris Rabb introduced legislation (H.B. 2767) that would establish an Equal Opportunity Audit program for contractors, grant recipients, and beneficiaries of tax incentives in Pennsylvania.
The proposed audit program would strengthen accountability and transparency for these entities through several requirements, including the enforcement of nondiscrimination policies and public disclosure of merit criteria for hiring and contracting decisions.
Sanctions for noncompliance may include suspension of contracts, recovery of grant funds, denial of tax incentives, or temporary disbarment. The bill has been referred to the PA House Intergovernmental Affairs and Operations Committee.
"With billions of dollars in public resources awarded by the commonwealth each year, it is imperative that entities demonstrate a genuine commitment to equal opportunity," Rabb said. "Currently, there is no system to evaluate their devotion to these principles, and the Equal Opportunity Audit program would provide that framework. We need to identify what a level playing field looks like, so that we can invest in the means to define it."
Alvin B. Tillery Jr., professor of political science and founding director of the Center for the Study of Diversity and Democracy at Northwestern University, developed a model that helped inform the bill. He said Rabb "has crafted a measure that is transparent, evidence-based, and workable for employers."
"H.B. 2767 is durable in a way federal policy no longer is," Tillery said. "It does not depend on an executive order that can be revoked or a reporting requirement that can be scrapped by rulemaking. It rests on the simplest principle in public administration: The commonwealth should know whether its contractors are treating people fairly."
More information about the legislation is available at
https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb2767
.

After a watchdog group filed a formal campaign finance complaint against political activist Scott Presler, state Rep. Jared Solomon highlighted the need to protect Pennsylvania voters with stronger penalties for campaign violations.
Solomon introduced legislation along with state Rep. Chris Rabb that would enhance penalties for any such violation.
The allegations against Presler stem from his voter registration work at Early Vote Action, where he allegedly did not disclose sources of revenue or detailed expenditures required by state campaign laws.
“The foundation for America’s election system lies right here in Pennsylvania. As elected officials, our constituents have trusted us to safeguard the security and integrity of our elections, ensuring that their votes count and their voices are heard. We must do so by being transparent and holding people accountable when they violate that trust.
“Unfortunately, there are distorted narratives, misinformation and sometimes blatant untruths being pushed into the commonwealth’s political landscape with significant financial resources that are not documented, registered or disclosed as campaign finance law requires. Pennsylvania voters should be able to walk into a voting booth, confident and informed in their chosen candidate,” Solomon said.
“There should be no out, no ‘cost of doing business’ for distorting the right of Pennsylvanians to choose their elected officials. I look forward to working with Rep. Solomon to ensure there is financial transparency in our election process, and to make clear that bad actors will not be tolerated in our political discourse,” Rabb said.
Solomon added that even when these “activists” are convicted, the penalties are so menial that they hardly serve as a deterrent and seem to be just a part of doing business.
The legislation would increase penalties for civil or criminal convictions from violating campaign finance laws and prohibit that person from holding a trusted position on any level of politics.
Solomon is a longstanding and staunch advocate of transparency and trust throughout all levels of government. He’s introduced legislation calling for transparency around dark money groups and gift bans for elected officials, promoting fairness in election ballot positions, and requiring all elected officials to resign upon conviction of any crime.

Rabb applauds legislation amending second-degree murder sentencing
Rep. Christopher M. Rabb
July 24, 2026 | 4:49 PM
HARRISBURG, July 24
– Today, state Rep. Chris Rabb applauds the House passage of H.B. 1042, amending second-degree murder sentencing following the Pennsylvania Supreme Court’s ruling on
Commonwealth v. Lee.
The bill would end the practice of mandatory life sentences for second-degree murder, in accordance with the Supreme Court’s decision on March 26. The bill would replace the automatic life without parole sentence for second-degree murder with sentencing linked to an offender’s level of culpability. It also lets people serving time in state prison earn vocational training and education credit toward limited sentence reduction, fostering better post-release outcomes, and saves taxpayer money by allowing petitions to release extremely ill people from prison.
“I’m pleased that the General Assembly has fulfilled its constitutional obligation to pass a sentencing framework that reflects individual culpability and aligns our laws with the basic principles of justice,” Rabb said. “Following the Supreme Court’s decree, we’re ending a one-size-fits-all punishment that treats people who never intended to kill the same as those who did. I’d like to thank all the advocates, organizers, researchers and Pennsylvanians impacted directly by this injustice; as they spoke up and refused to accept a system not rooted in fairness.”
Throughout his tenure in the legislature, Rabb has remained a steadfast advocate for reforming the state’s criminal legal system.
Rabb’s bill to end mandatory life without parole
for second-degree murder was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in November 2022 and was never brought up for a vote.
House Bill 1042 has been sent to the Senate for consideration.

HARRISBURG, July 15 –
Today, state Rep. Chris Rabb applauds the passage of the 2026-27 Pennsylvania state budget, including investments in affordability and stronger schools for all students.
The 2026-27 budget prioritizes everyday Pennsylvanians through initiatives like the Working Pennsylvanians Tax Credit, addressing rising energy costs, supporting reliable infrastructure and protecting consumers. The budget also requires large data centers to publicly report their energy and water usage, helping communities plan for future infrastructure needs.

I thank my friends in the House for continuing to stand up for our students.”
Other funding increases and new investments in the budget include:
$24.2 million for rape crisis response, which nearly doubles funding for that program.
A 20% increase for the childcare recruitment and retention program.
A 9.1% increase for early intervention services for children with developmental delays.
Increased oversight and transparency requirements for data centers.
$6 million for avian flu surveillance and response.

Rep. Christopher M. Rabb
June 18, 2026 | 4:33 PM
HARRISBURG, June 18 –
On June 17, legislation (H.B. 2443) amended by state Rep. Chris Rabb that would establish the Child Victim Recovery Fund advanced through the PA House of Representatives by a unanimous 202–0 vote.
House Bill 2443, sponsored by state Reps. Kyle Mullins and Jim Rigby, would create the recovery fund by imposing fees of $250 to $1,000 on individuals convicted of or placed into diversion programs for sexual crimes involving child victims. The fund would support child advocacy centers across Pennsylvania, which provide medical exams, therapy, and advocacy services for abused and exploited children.
Rabb’s amendment would require courts to consider a defendant’s ability to pay the Mandatory Child Victim Recovery Fee and allow for reductions if the fee is deemed excessive. It also would prohibit courts from setting mandatory minimum installment payments that are not based on ability to pay.
“I had stated publicly last month that I would support the bill if appropriately amended,” Rabb said. “The successful passage of this bill with my amendment affirms my pledge to ensure that establishment of such a fund is done in an equitable and sustainable manner.”

The bill would amend Pennsylvania law by strengthening penalties for trafficking infant children and creating a new sentencing consideration for defendants who were themselves victims of child abuse.
Regarding H.B. 1616, Rabb said:
“As a descendant of Black women, men, and children who were legally bought and sold under state-sanctioned slavery, my commitment to protecting children from exploitation is unwavering. I support the intent behind the bill’s sentencing-consideration provision, which recognizes that childhood victimization can influence the circumstances that lead some individuals into the criminal legal system. However, good intentions must be matched with clear safeguards.
“H.B. 1616 does not establish standards for how courts should weigh this factor, creating the potential for inconsistent application across courtrooms. In some cases, survivors who most deserve consideration could be denied relief; in others, the provision could be stretched beyond its intended purpose. I raised a similar concern in May regarding the infant-dealing provisions in H.B. 910. When laws lack clear parameters, they can end up harming the very people they are meant to protect.
“I could not, in good conscience, vote for a provision with such significant consequences without those safeguards in place.”
Throughout his five terms in the Pennsylvania House, Rabb has been a vocal advocate for survivor-centered criminal legal reform. He has consistently urged lawmakers to pair reform efforts with the structural safeguards necessary to ensure legislation is applied fairly and as intended.

Rabb legislation strengthening law enforcement misconduct database advances through committee
Rep. Christopher M. Rabb
June 17, 2026 | 11:03 AM
HARRISBURG, June 17 –
Today, legislation sponsored by state Rep. Chris Rabb (H.B. 131) to strengthen the state’s interdepartmental law enforcement misconduct database statute advanced through the House Judiciary Committee.
House Bill 131 would make changes to Act 57 of 2020 to further bolster transparency and accountability measures that were stripped from the original bill after a bipartisan, bicameral agreement to unanimously support the legislation without amendment.
Established in 2021, this statewide database is maintained by the Municipal Police Officers’ Education and Training Commission. Under current law, law enforcement agencies are required to enter any “final and binding” disciplinary actions into the database when an officer leaves employment. House Bill 131 would widen the scope of the database to include any substantive disciplinary action, as well as add penalties for non-compliance by law enforcement agencies.
“This database can be an invaluable resource for community safety, but only if we fulfill it to its highest potential,” Rabb said. “These changes will ensure no documented misconduct goes undetected and will deter law enforcement agencies from failing to take part in the accountability process. I urge the House to consider this and join the effort to make Pennsylvania a national model for police accountability.”

Rabb congratulates Philadelphia City Council on passing resolution supporting ranked choice voting
Rep. Christopher M. Rabb
June 2, 2026 | 10:25 AM
PHILADELPHIA, June 2 –
Today, state Rep. Chris Rabb congratulated the Philadelphia City Council for passing a resolution in support of ranked choice voting.
On May 28, council passed a resolution that calls on the Pennsylvania House of Representatives to pass legislation allowing cities and counties to use ranked choice voting in local elections. Ranked choice elections would give voters the option to rank candidates in order of preference.
House Bill 123, legislation introduced by Rabb and co-prime sponsor Rep. John Inglis in November 2025, would provide the authority to enact ranked choice voting in any primary, general or special election. The bill currently sits in the House State Government Committee.
“I applaud Philadelphia City Council for attempting to restore honesty and integrity back into the democratic process,” Rabb said. “With ranked choice, voters can make their voice heard based on who they want to choose, not who they think will win. Our current plurality voting system does not truly reflect the will of the people, as it prioritizes divisiveness over common priorities, and extremism over collaboration. I hope the council’s support for ranked choice is heard loud and clear in Harrisburg.”
For more information on House Bill 123, visit

Rabb bill to abolish death penalty moves through Judiciary Committee
Rep. Christopher M. Rabb
April 27, 2026 | 2:21 PM
HARRISBURG, APRIL 27 –
Today, state Rep. Chris Rabb’s legislation (
H.B 99
), which would abolish the death penalty in Pennsylvania, was voted out of the House Judiciary Committee.
The bill, referred to the committee in October 2025, would make Pennsylvania the 24th state to abolish the death penalty. It will now make its way to the House floor for consideration.
“I want to thank my colleagues on the committee for understanding the various negative aspects of capital punishment,” Rabb said. “Not only is the death penalty an ineffective deterrent to violent crime, but it also costs the state an incredible amount of money, time, and resources. The risk of continuing this unproductive practice far outweighs the few, if any, benefits.”
Rabb added that the Commonwealth has already executed people who were innocent of the crimes for which they were sentenced to death.
“Even if just one innocent life is taken at the hands of the state, that is too much for me to bear,” Rabb said. “I’m glad that my colleagues feel the same way, and I urge the House to consider this legislation.”
More information about H.B. 99 and the House Judiciary Committee can be found at
www.palegis.us/house/committees/60/judiciary

MT. AIRY, APRIL 15
– Today, state Rep. Chris Rabb announced that $500,000 in grant funding will be allocated to help restart Safe Steps Northwest, a violence prevention initiative in Mt. Airy, Germantown and East Germantown.

I’m encouraged by the work the Mt. Airy CDC will lead in our communities, and this funding will help bring large-scale block cleaning back in a powerful and visible way. I’m grateful to the Commission for its generous support of our district and for recognizing the importance of this work.”

Justice reform lawmaker eager to build legal framework following state Supreme Court ruling
Rep. Christopher M. Rabb
March 26, 2026 | 3:52 PM
HARRISBURG, March 26
– State Rep. Chris Rabb today applauded a landmark decision by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court striking down mandatory life-without-parole sentences for people convicted of second-degree murder and issued the following statement:
“Today, justice in Pennsylvania took a long-overdue step forward.
“The Pennsylvania Supreme Court has ruled that mandatory life without parole for second-degree murder is unconstitutional—ending a one-size-fits-all punishment that treated people who never intended to kill the same as those who did. This legal decision aligns with
legislation
I introduced in 2022 along with former state Representative Dan Miller, that sought to address this same injustice.
“This victory didn’t happen overnight. It was built over years by advocates, organizers, researchers, and Pennsylvanians impacted directly by this injustice who refused to accept a system untethered from fairness or proportionality.
“We owe deep gratitude to organizations like the Amistad Law Project, the Defender Association of Philadelphia, Philadelphia Lawyers for Social Equity, Families Against Mandatory Minimums, Decarcerate PA, and the Abolitionist Law Center—along with countless community leaders, House Speaker Joanna McClinton, Judiciary Chairman Tim Briggs, and incarcerated people and returning citizens whose voices made this moment possible.
“The court has spoken. Now the General Assembly must commit itself to act. We have a constitutional obligation—and a moral one—to build a sentencing framework that reflects individual culpability, ensures accountability, and finally aligns our laws with basic principles of justice.
“Now, let’s finish the job by passing Chairman Briggs’ legislation —
H.B. 443
— drafted by the
same team
that won the
Lee
case!”
Throughout his tenure in the legislature, Rabb has remained a steadfast advocate for reforming the state’s criminal legal system.
Rabb’s bill to end mandatory life without parole
for second-degree murder was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in November of 2022 and was never brought up for a vote.

Rabb: Hate crime laws are not enough to prevent violence
Lawmaker urges further reforms to address root causes of hate-based crimes
Rep. Christopher M. Rabb
March 11, 2026 | 10:19 AM
HARRISBURG, March 11
– State Rep. Chris Rabb voted to advance two anti-hate crime bills Tuesday in the Pennsylvania House Judiciary Committee, while reiterating his longstanding concerns that criminal penalties alone fail to address the underlying causes of and prevent hate-based violence.
“My votes on these bills reflect both my unequivocal opposition to hate crimes and my commitment to addressing the root causes of structural violence,” Rabb said. “Hate crimes are a painful and persistent reality in Pennsylvania, and we have a duty to respond to these heinous acts. Simultaneously, we must acknowledge the reality that simply increasing penalties after harm occurs is not effective at preventing attacks.”
During previous consideration of similar legislation, Rabb raised concerns about the effectiveness and unintended consequences of hate crime statutes,
worked to amend
the bills, and
asked broader questions
about how Pennsylvania addresses hate and violence.
“For those of us who support the intent of hate crime legislation, we should assess its limitations honestly. If we want to reduce hate-based violence, we must address the structural conditions that fuel it.”
House Bill 1902
would provide training to law enforcement to improve the identification, investigation and prevention of hate-based intimidation crimes, while
House Bill 1905
would update Pennsylvania’s ethnic intimidation law and strengthen penalties for bias-motivated offenses targeting individuals based on protected characteristics.
Rabb voted to approve both bills and said he will continue working with lawmakers, advocates and impacted communities to ensure Pennsylvania’s approach to addressing hate-based violence includes both accountability and meaningful prevention.

Two bills supporting local journalism approved in committee
Rep. Christopher M. Rabb
February 4, 2026 | 1:53 PM
HARRISBURG, Feb. 4
– The Pennsylvania House Communications and Technology Committee today advanced two bills aimed at supporting the development of local journalism across the commonwealth.
“For the past 20 years, we’ve seen a troubling decline in the number of local newspapers and reporters covering important community issues,” said state Rep. Joseph Ciresi, D-Montgomery.
“Thousands of newspapers have closed, and the number of newsroom employees has dropped by more than half. Local journalism in Pennsylvania needs support. The first weeks of 2026 underscore the urgency: the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette announced it will shut down, the Clinton County Record ceased publication, and the LNP Media Group in Lancaster, along with Lehigh Valley Public Media, announced significant layoffs.
“The decline in local news reporting is having a devastating impact on our democracy,” Ciresi added. “If residents don’t know what’s happening in their towns and cities, how can they understand what issues need attention or hold leaders accountable? An informed electorate is the foundation of an engaged one.”
Ciresi noted that the proposed bills aim to reduce news deserts by placing journalists in communities where they are needed most, preserving a strong local media environment across Pennsylvania.
Introduced by state Rep. Chris Rabb, D-Phila., the legislative package addresses the growing shortage of community-based news sources in the state.
House Bill 2047
would establish a state fellowship program for journalists in local news that would aim to replace local reporters that have left the industry or gone into early retirement.
The legislation is modeled on successful programs in California, Washington and New Mexico.
House Bill 2048
would establish the Pennsylvania Civic Information Consortium to support civic information and local journalism initiatives. The consortium could enter into an agreement with the State Library System, an institution within the State System of Higher Education, or another public institution to provide administrative services.
The legislation was inspired by the success of the New Jersey Civic Information Consortium.
“When local news disappears, communities lose transparency, accountability and a shared set of facts,” said Rabb. “These bills move us closer to treating civic information as the public good it is, by supporting the independent, nonpartisan journalism that functioning democracies rely on.”

Rabb welcomes leaders of federally recognized Tribal Nations to Capitol
Rep. Christopher M. Rabb
October 20, 2026 | 4:58 PM
HARRISBURG, Oct. 20 –
This week, state Rep. Chris Rabb welcomed leaders of federally recognized Tribal Nations with ancestral ties to Pennsylvania to the state Capitol.
Rabb brought the leaders to Harrisburg for recognition in the House chamber during Monday's session and to meet with lawmakers from across the commonwealth.
Guests included:
• Michael McLane, president of Delaware Nation
• Dr. Katelyn Lucas, historic preservation officer for Delaware Nation
• Chief Brad KillsCrow, chief of the Delaware Tribe of Indians
The Delaware Nation is a sovereign, federally recognized nation of Lenape people whose ancestral homelands have encompassed eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, and parts of New York, Connecticut and Maryland. The Delaware Tribe of Indians is a federally recognized tribe of the Lenape people with longstanding ties to the Delaware River region.
The guests visited to engage with Pennsylvania legislators on tribal sovereignty, government-to-government consultation, and the protection of Indigenous cultural heritage and burial sites.
"This is a historic occasion for our chamber, and I am grateful for the presence and expertise of these Tribal leaders as we foster greater dialogue around Indigenous legislation," Rabb said. "Legislation and policies affecting Indigenous communities must be informed by their voices, developed through meaningful consultation with their recognized leadership, and guided by their knowledge and perspectives."
Also this week, Rabb introduced House Resolution 671. It directs the Legislative Budget and Finance Committee to study the intergenerational impact of the Carlisle Indian Industrial School on Indigenous youth taken to Pennsylvania. The study would also examine the complicity of state government, religious institutions, academia, philanthropy and the private sector in a broader campaign of cultural genocide waged against Indigenous children across North America.
Founded in 1879, Carlisle was the first federal off-reservation Indian boarding school and the blueprint for a nationwide system built on its founder's creed: "Kill the Indian in him, and save the man." Children were separated from their families and stripped of their names, languages, clothing and spiritual traditions. Many never went home.
"Carlisle was not an educational experiment. It was an instrument of erasure, designed to sever Indigenous children from their families, their languages and their nations," Rabb said. "That happened here, on Pennsylvania soil, sustained by institutions that still exist today. We cannot atone for what we refuse to name. This study puts truth-telling first, led by Indigenous voices, so that any path toward atonement and healing rests on the full truth, not on euphemism."
